Agents (accessed through their CLIs at default settings): A1 Claude Code (Anthropic, Claude Opus with extended thinking); A2 Codex (OpenAI, the latest Codex model via GitHub Copilot); A3 Gemini Code Assist (Google, Gemini with the highest reasoning configuration). Prompt template per task: task title, description and functional requirements, plus framing: a complete project for a clean Ubuntu 22.04 machine with only the language runtime, including source code, a dependency file (requirements.txt, pom.xml, package.json or CMakeLists.txt) with all direct and transitive dependencies pinned to exact versions, and README.md with setup, build and run instructions (explicit variant, used for all runs)

Gen: agent produces code and manifest; Execute in an isolated Docker container; on failure, Repair with the runtime error, up to K = 10 cycles (max 11 interactions, full history kept); then extraction: ParseManifest (declared set D1 from the initial manifest), Resolve (installed set D2 via the package manager), Trace (runtime set D3 via Sciunit ptrace tracing)

None as review gates. All 1,000 instances executed manually: a human submits prompts, transfers artefacts to containers, transcribes runtime errors verbatim to the agent and records outcomes. Authors annotate standard-library-sufficient tasks and C++ failure types

Tasks: 50 tasks in Python, Java, JavaScript, C++. Configurations: three agents via CLI at default settings. Baseline: none (static tools such as pipreqs mentioned but not run). Held constant: identical prompt template (explicit variant) across agents and languages, repair budget K = 10, clean per-language Docker images, full history in repair. Acceptance: successful execution in the clean container; runtime trace as dependency ground truth. Repetitions: one run per agent-task-language, Claude Code two extra independent trials. Human intervention: manual execution with verbatim transcription of errors

No agent strong in all languages on first attempt (Claude and Codex strong in Python and JavaScript, weak in Java and C++; Gemini weakest in Python 32%, strongest in C++ 80%); after repair nearly all converge, but repair cost differs up to five-fold. Pooled F1: Python 0.765, Java 0.708, JavaScript 0.219, C++ 0.018. Cross-agent Jaccard below 0.5 in all languages, as low as 0.073 (Codex–Gemini, JavaScript); complete disjointness 36.0% (Python) to 63.3% (JavaScript), macro 53.3%. Claude never reproduces the same declared set across three trials (UCR 0%). Claude's C++ failures mostly system-library assumptions (87.5%). Spearman: larger manifests associated with lower first-attempt success in Python, Java, C++ (p ≤ 0.0013), not JavaScript (p = 0.256). No significance tests between agents

It distinguished agents and ecosystems on first-attempt success and dependency accuracy, where final success alone would rate all agents near-perfect. Repeatability: repeated Claude Code trials show dependency choices are not stable (intra-agent agreement near zero). Limitations of the method stated: tracing undercounts header-only and compile-time C++ dependencies and conditionally imported packages; C++ D1-vs-D2 comparison structurally uninformative; manual protocol and fixed annotations introduce judgment; results conditioned on one prompt template; snapshot of evolving agents

Limitations: C++ runtime tracing undercounts header-only and compile-time dependencies; 50 controlled tasks rather than real-world projects; results conditioned on the prompt template (implicit variant not run, so rates are lower bounds); manual evaluation and annotations introduce judgment; agents evolve, so results are a snapshot. Gaps: benchmarks measure functional correctness but not environment specification; agent manifests are not trustworthy SBOM or audit artefacts; need for training objectives, evaluation frameworks and validation pipelines targeting accurate and minimal dependency specification

Inconsistencies: abstract claims 'newer agents show no meaningful improvement', but no comparison of agent generations is reported in the results. Paper calls 1,000 runs '1,000 curated/verified project instances' (600 primary + 400 trials). Table 5 UCR denominators are 48 (Java) and 35 (C++) although Claude reaches 100% final success in every language; not explained. Section 3.1 says a prompt is valid if code passes an accompanying test suite, but functional test results are not reported (success = runs without error). The C++ baseline subtraction is said to be defined in Section 3 but is not. Repair budget said to be set in agents' configuration files although runs were manual. Claim that 50 tasks give statistical power is not supported by a power analysis. Duplicated sentence in Section 5. Values from Tables 4-6 and text. Data: setup and extracted dependencies 'will be made available as an open reproducible artifact'; no link. No pre-registration. Languages studied: Python, Java, JavaScript, C++. Extends the authors' earlier study [11]; Sciunit is a tool co-authored by T. Malik
